references.text: The promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth shall be blessed in him points forward to people from every corner of the world gathering in God's kingdom ([ref:Gen 12:3|Genesis 12:3]).
Isaiah's prophecy that all nations will stream to the mountain of the Lord, and many peoples will go up to it, foretells the universal gathering that Jesus describes ([ref:Isa 2:2-3|Isaiah 2:2-3]).
The shoot from the root of Jesse shall stand as a banner for the nations, and the nations shall seek him—a prophecy about the inclusion of Gentiles in God's kingdom ([ref:Isa 11:10|Isaiah 11:10]).
The Lord promises to bring His people from east and west, from north and south—the same four corners of the earth that Jesus mentions ([ref:Isa 43:5-6|Isaiah 43:5-6]).
The prophecy that people will come from far away, from north and west and from the land of Sinim, reflects the idea of nations gathering from every direction ([ref:Isa 49:12|Isaiah 49:12]).
From the west they shall fear the name of the Lord, and from the rising of the sun His glory—a universal acknowledgment of God from all directions ([ref:Isa 59:19|Isaiah 59:19]).

Malachi prophesies that from the rising of the sun to its setting, the Lord's name shall be great among the nations—a clear parallel to nations coming from east and west ([ref:Mal 1:11|Malachi 1:11]).
The psalmist describes those whom the Lord has gathered from the lands, from east and west, from north and south—exactly the four cardinal directions Jesus mentions ([ref:Psa 107:3|Psalms 107:3]).

Jesus' parallel statement in the Gospel of Matthew that many will come from east and west and sit at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven ([ref:Matt 8:11-12|Matthew 8:11-12]).

John's vision of a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne—the fulfillment of the promise of universal salvation ([ref:Rev 7:9|Revelation 7:9]).
Isaiah describes the eschatological feast the Lord will prepare for all peoples on this mountain—the background for the image of sitting at the table in God's kingdom ([ref:Isa 25:6|Isaiah 25:6]).

The parable of the great banquet in Luke expands on the theme of who ultimately takes their places at the table in God's kingdom, where those first invited refuse, and others are brought in ([ref:Luk 14:15-24|Luke 14:15-24]).
